summary: Defines the use case for Infrastructure ENUM and proposes a parallel namespace to e164.arpa as a long-term solution. It would let carriers publish DNS records for telephone numbers independently of those created by the number holders.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone companies want their own address book for phone numbers, separate from the one customers can edit. This note proposes a second listing just for them.

questions: why do carriers need separate enum
subtitle: A separate namespace for carriers to publish phone number routing information.

tldr.problem: Phone companies need to publish DNS records for phone numbers independently from the records that phone number owners can create, but the standard ENUM system is based on end-user control.
tldr.mechanism: This proposal creates a parallel DNS namespace to e164.arpa specifically for carrier use, allowing carriers to manage their own records separately from end users.
tldr.outcome: Service providers can now publish ENUM information for VoIP interconnection without requiring individual user enrollment or coordination.

today: RFC 5526 remains an Informational document. It proposes the use case and architecture for Infrastructure ENUM but does not define the exact namespace. The proposal influenced later work on carrier-based ENUM systems.

sections.title: What Infrastructure ENUM Does
sections.content:
ENUM is a system that turns phone numbers into domain names and looks up DNS records to find the services available for that number. The standard ENUM system (RFC 3761) is based on end-user enrollment: individuals can create their own records. However, phone companies need a way to publish ENUM information for their phone numbers without waiting for millions of users to opt in.

Infrastructure ENUM solves this by letting carriers publish DNS records for the phone numbers they serve, enabling VoIP calls to be routed directly over IP networks without touching the old telephone network.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone companies want a way to tell the internet where calls should go, separate from what customers publish.

sections.title: Why Carriers Need It
sections.content:
The original ENUM system required end-user opt-in, which works for individuals but not for carriers managing large blocks of phone numbers. Carriers could demand that users enroll through contracts, but this creates practical problems: it puts control in the hands of individual users, it does not work for number portability tracking, and it does not serve the carriers' own infrastructure needs.

VoIP networks benefit most when calls stay on IP networks end-to-end. Infrastructure ENUM lets carriers publish the interconnection points where VoIP calls should route, reducing transcoding and enabling new IP-based services.
sections.plainLanguage: Waiting for millions of people to sign up is slow and messy. Phone companies need to control their own information.

sections.title: The Parallel Namespace
sections.content:
This RFC proposes a new DNS namespace parallel to e164.arpa, dedicated to Infrastructure ENUM. The carrier-of-record for a given E.164 phone number controls the Tier 2 records in this infrastructure tree. Each country or numbering authority defines who the carrier-of-record is.

Existing Enumservices registered with IANA remain valid for both end-user and infrastructure ENUM, so the system is compatible with established practices.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of changing the main phone number directory, this creates a separate directory just for carriers to manage.
